Three days ago, the Indian sycamorcs, on
the roads to Heliopois and Shoobra, stood
perfectly cold and naked to-day they arc
vailed In the brightest drapcry of young
leaves. The buds of the poplar and mul
berry trees, also, are opening so fast that
one can fairly notice a change from hour
to hour. But this is April, in land
where February was wont to be the
Spring month.


1t is difficult to estimate the character
OF a development which depends upon the
will Of one man. With the wonderful
spectacle Of Japan before our eyes, we
may easily be misled by the external signs
of change in Egypt. In Japan, however,
the experiment is tried upon a curious,
restless and quickwitted people, whose re.
ligious faith, tolerant because phllosophic,
interposes uo serious hinderauce to their
advance in civilization. Here, the condi-
tions are very different; every change re.
qulres care and caution, aud old prejudices
have even greater force than personal
interest. From all can learn, the re-
cent development of Egypt is chiefly ma
terial, due in great measure to the de-
sire for show and gain of a ruler who Is
shrowd, intelligent, practical in business
matters, and personally ambitious. 1t is
too much to expect that an Oriental prince,
in our day, shall manifest hearty inter-
est hearty interest in the well-being OF
his subjects. The Egyptians complain Bit
tcrly of three evils. which to them more
than couuterbalance the advantages
thrust upon them. These are: enormous
taxes, utter lack Of defense against the
arbitrary will Of those set over them, and
the negligence and corruption of both civil
and criminal courts.


Until the last two or three years,
Egyptian statistics have been very con-
fused and uutrustworthy. 1t is therefore
difficult to make any satisfactory compar-
sons. The people compare the Khetive's S
Government with that of his predecessor,
Said Pasha 1854 to 1869, which gave
them justice, security, and only moderate
burdens and they seem to forget what
they previously endured under Abbas
Pasha, and during the last years Of Mo-
hammcd Ais rdign. The latter with all
his tremendous energy and keen political
wisdom, was a selfish despot. He origi-
mated method of taxation which would
have ruined Egypt had it not been changed
"a bounty or date palms, amounting to
seven or eight cents tree. During my
journey in E,hiopa, in 1852, this tax had
just been increased, and in some districts
the people ru,hlessly destroyed their palm
groves in order to evade it. The tax has
now been converted into cne upon real
estate, which is so high that ah acre plsnt-
ed with date-palms costs at the rate Of 20
cents tree. The cost of labor and food
has also incr1 r1ased it is true, but in moth:
ing like the same proportion. When,
therefore, The people see the Khedive
spending, in few weeks, $l5 900, 900
for the marriage festivities Of his sons I;
when they see enormous palaces building
for these sons, while score or two of
royal residences are standing empty when
thev hear that the Goveroment is hard up
for money, while jewels are purchased
and foreign opera troups brought to Cairo
regardless of expense it is not much
wonder if they become impatient. Igno.
rant as they are, verify believe the
F most of them would submit more readily
TO their burdens, if the revenues of Egypt
we're bestowed mainly on necessary public
works.


The people, moreover, are etill suffer-
ing from great initiation and reaction
which is curiously connected with their
own internal struggle. The cotton crop
of Egypt had been steadily, but
rather slowly, increasing, up to 1860,
when it reached about 10000 bales.
The breaking out Of the Rebellion gave
tremendous impetus to this branch of pro-
duction: the sudden rise in the value of
cotton made it more profitable than wheat
or sugar-cane. All over Egypt the cuti-
vation spread the shrewd agriculturists,
who foresaw their chance. made such prof
its that the small Fellah farmers even
pulled up their maize and onions, and
planted cotton. BY 1864 the production

market price $50 per cent higher than
in 1860


For the first time perhaps IN thousands
Of years, Egypt did not produce enough

corn and even fodder for cattle were ip.-

Three days ago, the Indian sycamores, on
the roads to Heliopolis and Shoobra, stood
perfectly cold and naked; to-day they are
veiled in the brightest drapery of young
leaves. The buds of the poplar and mul-
berry trees, also, are opening so fast that
one can fairly notice a change from hour
to hour. But this is April, in a land
where February was wont to be the
Spring month.


It is difficult to estimate the character
of a development which depends upon the
will of one man. With the wonderful
spectacle of Japan before our eyes, we
may easily be misled by the external signs
of change in Egypt. In Japan, however,
the experiment is tried upon a curious,
restless and quickwitted people, whose re-
ligious faith, tolerant because philosophic,
interposes no serious hindrance to their
advance in civilization. Here, the condi-
tions are very different; every change re-
quires care and caution, and old prejudices
have even greater force than personal
interest. From all can learn, the re-
cent development of Egypt is chiefly ma-
terial, due in great measure to the de-
sire for show and gain of a ruler who is
shrewd, intelligent, practical in business
matters, and personally ambitious. It is
too much to expect that an Oriental prince,
in our day, shall manifest hearty inter-
est in the well-being of his subjects. The Egyptians complain
bitterly of three evils, which to them more
than counterbalance the advantages
thrust upon them. These are: enormous
taxes, utter lack of defense against the
arbitrary will of those set over them, and
the negligence and corruption of both civil
and criminal courts.


Until the last two or three years,
Egyptian statistics have been very con-
fused and untrustworthy. It is therefore
difficult to make any satisfactory compar-
isons. The people compare the Khedive's
Government with that of his predecessor,
Said Pasha 1854 to 1869, which gave
them justice, security, and only moderate
burdens; and they seem to forget what
they previously endured under Abbas
Pasha, and during the last years of Mo-
hammed Ali's reign. The latter with all
his tremendous energy and keen political
wisdom, was a selfish despot. He origi-
nated a method of taxation which would
have ruined Egypt had it not been changed—
"a bounty on date palms, amounting to
seven or eight cents per tree. During my
journey in Ethiopia, in 1852, this tax had
just been increased, and in some districts
the people ruthlessly destroyed their palm
groves in order to evade it. The tax has
now been converted into one upon real
estate, which is so high that an acre plant-
ed with date-palms costs at the rate of 20

less the same proportion. When,
therefore, the people see the Khedive
spending, in few weeks, $15,900 for the marriage festivities of his sons;

for money, while jewels are purchased

INAUGURATIONS.
MADISON, Jan. 5.—The inauguration ceremony occurred at noon, to-day. All the new state officers, and such old officers as could be present, assembled in the executive Office, which with the ante-rooms and corridors was crowded with persons.
The old state officers at the hour appointed, escorted Gov. Taylor and associates to the Assembly chamber, where they took the oath of Office. The ceremony was quietly performed, and occupied but half an hour.

APPOINTMENTS.
The following appointments are announced: Private Secretary to the Governor, W. Bird, of Jefferson.

Col. Robert Cowdin, who died in Boston on
Wednesday was one of the old residents of that city
and served creditably in the Civil War. Being in com-
mand of the 1st Regiment of State militia when hostilities began, he immediately volunteered in
June 1861 proceeded with his regiment in
Massachusetts to Washington, going through Baltimore through which no troops had passed since
the 9th, were assailed in April. Col. Cowdin and his
regiment began the fighting at Blackburn's Ford and at
the battle of Bull Run. He was the most
conspicuous man in the regiment at the fight,
fought in his shirt sleeves and at the head of his company, in
one instance having ordered the men to lie down under
heavy fire from the enemy, he alone remained standing
and remarked "The bullet is not cast that can hit
me today." Being addressed by some person on the
left, he raised his hat, when a bullet from the
right side shattered a tree directly behind him.
The Colonel quietly replied "I am certain that bullet is not yet cast that can hit me"
and then gave orders as cool as if on dress.
The regiment retreated only under
Gen. Richardson. Had Col. Cowdin stayed supported as he
wished, it is believed the enemy would not have
driven him. Having recovered from his part in the engagement, Col. Cowdin resumed some duties in the service, and a warm
reception was accorded him by his comrades of the war.
On May 18, 1861, Col. Cowdin showed his zeal in
defending the Union.


CAPT. HENRY RANDALL


Capt. Henry Randall, a veteran steamship
commander, and for many years well known to the ship
merchants of New-York and its vicinity, died at his
residence No. 70 East Twenty-third early Wednesday
morning. He was at Berlin, in this state. In 1852
he exhibited decided fondness for the sea
and talent for navigation. He became stevedore and
rapidly advanced from obscure position on shipboard,
becoming the
commander of the steamboat Empire, which ran
like Erie. A few years later he was placed in com-
mand of the steamship Winona. He was one of the
steamers dispatched from New York to the West
coast. He was afterward resident of New York,
in the shipping trade, but at length settled in
California, where he remained several years. He again
appeared in New-York and soon as well as ever,
he never carried into execution the dream of his life, though a few months previous his death he
was more determined than ever before pursuing his in-
terest. He obtained from the last character
of a steamship company whose vessels were to be
built on the plan which he had proposed. It
was far from an organization.
He was a man strict in duty and much energy and
decision of character and had thus used his life.


COL. T. H. STANLEY


Col. Timothy H. Stanley, who died on Wednesday,
was a long-time resident of New York, and also an influential supporter of the Republican party.

We find in the Shreveport Times of the lot

inst, the following paragraph:

Several days have passed since the publication of the Address of the Democratic Central Committee, and yet the BULLETIN and Picayune have, so far, evaded any expression of opinion in relation to it. The people of this State, outside of New Orleans, want to know whether the BULLETIN and Picayune are going to support the action of the Committee or repudiate it; in other words, whether or no their idea of a successful campaign in Louisiana and the redemption of the State, like that of Mr. Emile LaSere and the other New Orleans ring masters, is the electing of their partisans to the city offices, and that this must be accomplished, even to the sacrifice of all the balance of the State? Our people want clear and explicit explanation from these papers on this matter.

Had our contemporary read the columns of the BULLETIN attentively, he would not have fallen into the blunder he has, so far as we are concerned. Simultaneously with the publication of the address of the Democratic State Central Committee, we commented editorially upon it, and gave it our sanction and support. To this extent our people have had "a clear and explicit explanation" from us. Now we propose to address ourselves to the Shreveport Times:

We sincerely regret to see so able and influential a Journal as the Times like its namesake in this city, lending its columns to distract the people and create dissension. Dissatisfied simply because the Democratic Convention is to assemble in New Orleans, it proposes now to call another convention, to be held in Alexandria on the 15th of September. And for what purpose? To please the Shreveport Times man, who has taken umbrage at the fact that the Democratic party has taken the initial step to organize for the campaign. If the effort to call another convention succeeds, it will result simply in organizing a party that will bring defeat to the great cause for which we are all striving.

We were not aware that the White League intended to constitute itself a political party. The purpose of the organization, as we understood it, was simply a union of the white people for the defense of their families and homes, in view of the existence of black leagues. The necessity of a White League is obvious to the dullest comprehension, but, being for defensive purposes, it must be non-partisan. The moment it is made a political party its efficiency is impaired, and besides it is launched upon a sea of political troubles. That it can be made effective in campaign one will doubt, but the wise and discreet will see the impropriety of its introducing as its cardinal political element its popular doctrine, which is based entirely upon an issue of race.

Now, so far as the BULLETIN is concerned, we are laboring for the success of the white people and the defeat of the negro and the Republican party in this State. It is a matter of little import whether the battle be fought under the banner of the Democracy or any other, provided the hope of victory is held out, and the triumph of the great principle which we espouse is promised. The place for holding the convention is likewise immaterial. All we desire is the nomination of good, honest and capable men.

We are satisfied, however, that this work can only be accomplished by thorough and complete organization and in the most perfect harmony. We deplore, therefore, every attempt to sow the seeds of discord among the people by such democratic conduct as that of the Shreveport Times. We indulge the hope that our contemporary will, when he fully recognizes the mischief he is doing, gracefully yield his personal preferences and prejudices for the sake of the cause which we believe he has supported as fully as much as we have.

We wish to disabuse the mind of our sister city that New Orleans has any sinister designs on the convention, or wishes in any way to control it. The country members of the Committee insisted upon having it to meet here, and whilst we might have preferred to have some country place selected, it is now too late to make any change.

We appeal then, to all of the good people of Louisiana, to resolve that they will be perfectly united. Let them resolve to frown down every effort of demagogues and office-seekers to organize cliques and rings for the promotion of their individual interests. Let the watchword be the redemption of Louisiana and the restoration of good government.

sions, is the best pledge yet offered of re-
stored, happy and united Americanism. I am
sure that in our effort to rescue the State, we
will have the cordial support of the public
opinion and press of the North; but more im-
portant, because more immediate than these,
the aid of the Federal Executive.


President Grant can do more for the speedy
restoration of the State than all other influen-
ces from without; and although I have no po-
litical information, other than such as is com-
mon in not having access to the papers of the
day, still, from the perusal of these, I entertain
strong hopes he will not withhold his great in-
fluence from so good a work. There is no
overt hostility to his administration in any part
of the South, certainly none of any sort in an
organized form in this State. On the contrary,
the Conservative element look to him as their
chief, if not only hope of good government.
Congress has been appealed to, and is powe-
less to remedy the evils under which we suffer.
The judiciary can afford no relief for it has no
jurisdiction. The Executive alone can consti-
tutionally and legally assist us. It would be
the crowning glory of Gen. Grant's adminis-
tration to effect reconstruction, and restore
to the plundered and ruined States of the South
the blessings of good government and the op-
portunity to enjoy and to contribute to the fu-
ture prosperity of the country. I cannot think
that he will be indifferent, and I know how
gratefully his aid would be appreciated by our
suffering South Carolinians. Could he be
brought face to face with the monstrous evils
which degrade and oppress us, nothing could
prevent him from employing every prerogative
of his vast power to crush them out forever.


After all, however, our relief depends mostly
upon our own people. Let them organize and
consolidate all honest men who can rise above
unworthy prejudices and party slavery, to res-
cue the State from anarchy, ruin, and, in the
end, bloody despair. Respecting the Republ-
ican principles of the colored citizens, we should
earnestly seek their cooperation in the move-
ment. The State has been plunged into this
ruin by the rapacity and dishonesty of their
trusted leaders, who have brought shame and
obloquy upon the party, whose honor and in-
terests were in their keeping, and trampled
upon every right and interest of the whole peo-
ple in their insatiate greed for plunder. They
owe the State some reparation for the past, and
we surely have hope that there are some thou-
sands having sufficient honesty, intelligence
and patriotism to join the hue and cry against
the robber band.


Not many would be required, for the true
majority of the Radicals has always been ex-
aggerated. The whites have never been fully
polled since the war, and the ballot has never
been free from frauds. To secure such co-ope-
ration the honest colored people should be in
full share of all public offices. Power entrusted to us should be administered with-
out favor or prejudice, so as to secure the best
interests of the whole people, protect equally
in enjoyment of his just rights every cit-
izen, however high or humble, and promote the
welfare of all alike so far as may come within
the legitimate sphere of government.


Upon such principles only can harmony and
good government be secured in the present
state of society here. Cooperation in this
good work would lead to mutual dependence,
respect and good will, and tend more to the
elevation and development of the colored peo-
ple than all other possible expedients.


I consider these views worth pondering at
this time with reference to the taxpayers'
movement and the promised reform in the Re-
publican party. Of course the policy of the
people can only be settled by conventions of
their authorized representatives, but it is well
to take counsel together, and to interchange
views beforehand, in order that the public
mind may settle down upon such measures as
may be approved after due considerations. I
firmly believe the hour of deliverance is at
hand if we but be true to ourselves. Indeed,

In the great iron center of Pittsburg, large sums have been spent in experiments having for their object the production of Russian sheet, and Pittsburg skill and enterprise have at last solved the problem of all who have devoted their time and energies to this subject. Mr. W. D. Wood, of the New Keesport Iron Works, has alone been successful. After twenty years of study, labor and experiment, he succeeded in producing sheet iron equal in every respect to that of the Russian make, excepting that he could not give it that planished or hammered appearance, which adds so much to the beauty of the surface, and which is the chief characteristic of the imported article. It would be tedious to enumerate the various plans and processes which he has devised in order to give his sheets the desired "finishing touch." He resorted to all sorts of hammering schemes, but for a time found that the more he hammered the less satisfactorily were the results. With wonderful perseverance he hammered away until he struck the talismanic blow. The process, too, is so simple, so free from complication as to be almost rudimentary, and with hundreds of others who have produced great results from simple mechanical agencies, it was to him a matter of great surprise that he had not made the discovery years before. It is hardly possible to take up your journal during the summer and autumn without seeing either items or extended accounts of what horses have accomplished in trotting or running. We scarcely ever see accounts of their endurance in hauling loads at a given pace, or the number of miles they have accomplished in a given number of hours at a walking gait and yet this practically is of far more importance than their endurance at speed.

Agricultural fair managers, who might not inaptly be called "agricultural horse-trot managers" advertise widely the large amounts devoted as premiums for trotting and running, but not one word as to horses exhibiting the greatest endurance and speed at a walking gait. Why not? "Oh, it will not draw the crowd." Very well if agricultural fairs are simply intended to draw that class of humanity whose end and aim in life is trotting and running horses, and betting thereon, very well and good.

There is, however, now and then an individual who, while he admires this noble animal at speed, very well knows that this eternal pandering to mere speed is not only vitiating the taste of the public, but also is tending to breed out other valuable traits that cannot be spared.

A good walking horse should make, at that gait, an average of four miles an hour. How many can do it? Very few. Why so? The walking gait has ceased to be cultivated.

By the careful training of ambitious and active horses they may be made to walk five miles an hour as easily as the ordinary horse now walks three. There is no reason why an average pace of four miles an hour should not be kept up with ordinary loads throughout the day. The District of Columbia Investigating Committee

Claims to-day favors paying the citizens of Fred-
erick, Maryland, $50,000 reimbursement for contri-

for not on legal grounds but as an act of grace in vie

being that at the time the Confederates entered the city the
Maryland troops were absent fighting in the Union
army.

Augustine, Fla. The bill reserves to Congress the right

penses of the United States Courts in the Western Dis-

solidation of the Western and Eastern Districts, and

This wire is carried down by means of a six-pound iron shot, which becomes detached as soon as it strikes the bottom. The copper cup which brings up the sand is attached directly over the shot, and is invariably brought up filled with mud, sand or ooze which is generally very fine, the color varying in different localities, but usually partaking of a light olive. THE Mennonites, who have for the past
year been inspecting various portions Of the
West, finally made a purchase Of one hun
bred thousand acres of land in Kansas, few
days since. This peculiar people, with their
peculiar religious notions, left Russia for
this country from love of liberty, and for
conscience sake. Some months since col
ony of them settled in Manitoba, but they
have not been pleased with that locality
and they are changing their abode to Da-
kota along the line os the Red river


The Dakota and Kansas people are well
pleased with these new accessions to their
population 1t is said no better class of
immigrants has landed on our shores for
many years. They are sober, strong advo-
Gates Of peace, being opposed to war, oaths
and capital punishment, and noted for their
industrious habits. They leave the father
land because they are not willing to do mil
itary duty. BY special favor from En-
peror Paul, they were exempted from that
duty but this favor having been annuled,
they looked to America for the greater
freedom they desire. The ruling Emperor,
however, being unwilling to see his subjects
turning their backs upon their native land,
hoped to check the emigration by re-estab-
fishing the decree releasing them from mill
tary service, And while this action may
tend to pacify some of those who have not
yet made arrangements to Join their Ameri-
can colonies, it is likely the new and fertile
lands of the West will be so full of attrac-
tions as to largely add to these settlements.

Leary of the City Hall Precinct to special duty in the
Mayor's office.

William Moore, age 43, of No. 435 West
Thirty-ninth-st., committed suicide while temporarily
throwing himself from Thirty-ninth-st. into the North River.

Charles Klaer of No. 1877 Forsyth-st. was ar-
rested and released on $500 bail in suit against him
by Louis Brudenein of No. 60 Delancey St. to recover
damages for inducing his wife and children to
leave him.

Henry Linn, the auctioneer against whom a
complaint was made at the Mayor's office for misre-
presenting the wares sold, has made restitution to Mrs.
McGinn, the complainant, of $35, the amount of which
she claimed to have been defrauded.

Henry B. Hyde, who for a long time has
been Vice-President of the Equitable Insurance Com-
pany, was elected yesterday to the office of President,
the office having left vacant by the death of Col.
William C. Alexander on Sunday, Aug. 29.

Alderman Morris states that the proper
authorities will soon begin an unsparing warfare against
all banners, signs and other advertisements that are
displayed in the stop line. It is said
that the owners of such signs can be fined each day.

Capt. Noel of the British brig Peerless was
arrested yesterday by the sheriff's officers and held in
$4,000 bail in suit brought against him by one of his
passengers while a voyage from the West Indies to this port.

The Commissioners of the Sinking Fund
met yesterday, and on account of the absence of
a quorum adjourned till to-day, when the question
of building a new armory for the 9th Regiment will
come up. The Board of Aldermen will meet this after-
noon.

The Fire Commissioners at their meeting
yesterday awarded the contract for building an engine
house in East Sixty-seventh-st. to Thomas Duffy, price,
$5,100. The contract for furnishing the Department with
coal and wood until Jan. 1910, was awarded to Samuel
J. Freund at $15,605.

The usual Thursday evening reunion will be
held at the Free Training School at No. 11 East Tenth
st. at 8 o'clock this evening. Mme. de Ryther will sing,
Mrs. Dr. J. J. O'Brien will read humorous selections,
and Dr. Hull will make an address. All workingwomen
are invited to be present.

At a meeting on Tuesday of the Board of
Directors of the National Rifle Association it was
decided to make the price of admission to the
Creedmoor after Sept. 20 cents and 50 cents the
day of the International match. The time for opening
the prizes has been changed to Sept. 29.

There were 100 fires during August, involv-
ing loss of $35,050 upon which there was insurance
of $300,500. The loss of buildings amounted to $5,145;
insurance, $1,907 upon stock, $1,600 insurance, $9,150.
In August 1873 there were 101 fires, involving loss
of $15,912 upon which there was insurance of $9,850.

The sidewalk of East Twenty-third-st., near
Lexington-ave., is in condition most distressing to
needless pedestrians. The flagstones overlap in such
manner as to trip unwary feet. A gentleman measured
a lady with a child in her arms; she bruised herself by
falling in the same place.

Patrick Reardon, age 45, of No. 113 Baxter
St., in quarrel with James Craig at Hester and Eliza-
beth sts. last night, was shot at by him and narrowly
escaped instantaneous death. The bullet struck the side
of his head and glanced off, inflicting a severe scalp
wound. Craig escaped. Police Surgeon Crane dressed
Reardon's wound and then had the man conveyed home.

At a hearing in the case of Winship, the
defendant yesterday, by Levi A. Fuller, referee, Frederick
Ogden, banker, testified that in October, 1870, he
was Assistant Auditor in the Customhouse, and paid
thereof probably about $4,000. The profits of the
business large but the losses also were considerable.

An inquest was held yesterday in the case of
George Sherman, age 8, who was struck by a Third
ave. car on Aug. 2 while attempting to steal a ride.
The jury exonerated the driver and conductor of the
car, and recommended that railroad officials and the
police authorities take measures to prevent the habit of
small boys of jumping on all parts of cars to steal a ride
of a few blocks.

Yesterday was the third day of the Bavarian
Festival at the Harlem River Park. The only new
feature of the merry-making was the opening of the
Dockauer Bank for the benefit of the German Hospital
in Seventy-ninth-st. To those who deposited a dollar,
interest of 1000 per cent, which is to fall due when
Bismarck becomes Pope of Rome.

A correspondent of a statistical turn of mind
complains of people who smoke on the front platform
of Second and Third ave. cars and concludes with the
following:

and August, I rode three lines 80 times, and on
50 of these occasions saw smoking in about 25
of 80 cases called the conductor's attention to
smokers, but no effort was made to stop the nuisance.

The largest company of Mennonites which
ever landed in this country arrived yesterday by the
steamship Teutonia from Hamburg. The number arrv-
ing by the steamer 1,010 and about 100 came
via Bremen also from Hamburg. So heavy were the
demands made upon the steamship company that an
extra steamer was supplied, the Teutonia being that
steamer. The Mennonites remained in Castle Garden
last night and will leave the city for Dakota to-day.

William H. Tillinghast of Burlington, N. J.,
came to this city with his son, William Tillinghast, age
15, yesterday, and after taking his son to a friend's
house, departed to transact some business. The son
was wandering through the city until night-
fall, when he accosted an officer of the Fifteenth Precinct and
informed him that he was lost. The officer took the boy
to Police Headquarters where up to a late hour last
night he had not been reclaimed by his father.

A meeting of the Importers and Grocers'
Board of Trade held at the office of the Association
yesterday afternoon. The President, Wm. A. Booth,
occupied the chair. W. H. Moses elected a member
of the organization, and the following Standing
Committees appointed:

COMMITTEE Canal, Railroads and Internal
F. Humphreys, Solomon Townsend, B. R. Buter, R. B.
Thurber, Page, shipping, Wharves, Docks and
Quarantine—D. A. Tafnare, W. H. Fox, William C. Boo, L. B.
Murphy, Harvey Harrington.

Nearly 800 convalescent patients of Bellevue
Hospital had their excursion yesterday. At 8 A. M. the
steamer Bellevue took them on board and steamed
away to Ward's Island. At the school ship salute was
fired and the boys manned the yards in honor of their
visitors. Warden Brennan was ubiquitous, and to his
exultation the success of the trip is in the man, due
to him. That luncheon was bountifully distributed and
many thanks were showered upon him kind.

our shores, far away towards the icy north.

steppes; wild ravines, clear and picturesque
lakes; immense forests of white birch and
fir trees; gigantic and superb glaciers. It is

you. The rivers of this great country, in

upon them. I have told you of the lead-
ing features of the country, topographical
ly considered; let me now say a few words
about the people, their mode of living,
their code of morality. I have been an
extensive traveller, but never in all my
experience have I met with such an hon-
est and simple class of people as the in-
habitants of Norway, Sweden and Lap-
land. Their faith in human nature is
something incredible, and their honesty
exceeds all bounds. Often have I left my
money behind me in farmhouse, and I
often have been followed on the road by
my late host with the treasure forgot in
his domicile. They scorn to take any re-
ward for doing what they consider their
duty, and as often as I have offered them
rewards they have been rejected. They

democratic people. Of their religious
simplicity volumes could be written.

testants or Lutherans. They bury their

notes. The light was thrown upon his

face: with a loud scream Kate rushed

toward him. The burglar was Tom

North. In a moment he had again passed

through the window, leaving the safe

open and the documents which he had

extracted strewn upon the table. Kate

had now fallen down almost insensible.

Just as Farmer North, who had been

aroused by her screams, rushed from

his bedroom, gun in hand, quickly

leaning from the state of the room

that the safe had been opened, and its

contents purloined, and also perceiving

at a glance that the window was open,

he rushed that way, the better, as he

thought, to track the culprit. About

a hundred yards from the house, he

thought he saw a figure quickly re-

treating in the distance. Without de-

liberating for more than an instant,

North fired his gun, and ran, as he

hoped, upon his game; but he could

find no intruder dead or alive. Re-

turning to the house, the farmer found

Kate Meadows in a state of the most

distressing agitation; but he could not

gather any further information from

her, that she had seen a man enter the

room and plunder the safe. When

pressed to answer if she could identify

him, she was too truthful to equivo-

cate, and implored him through her

tears not to ask her any more about the

incident of that most terrible night.


Farmer North having made every-

thing secure, and having assured his

wife, in one of those humane misre-

presentations of which it may be hoped

the recording angel will take no note,

that he had only gone out on hearing

the dogs bark, retired to rest. But he

was too keen an observer not to have

perceived that Kate Meadows had re-

cognised the burglar, who had shown

an intimate knowledge of the farm.

Governor of said State hereby gives a reward of one hundred dollars for the arrest and conviction of any person guilty of miscounting and a reward of Two hundred dollars for conviction of any person guilty of a felony in the violation of any of the provisions of an Act of the Legislature of this state, entitled "An Act relating to elections" approved March 1, 1873.

Rewards issuable for the arrest and conviction of any person against said Legislative act are authorized directed to be paid until the total amount specified reaches the sum of ten thousand dollars.

The subject sections of the Act relating to elections describe the offenses therein contained:

SEC. 1. Every person who makes, offers or accepts any wager upon the result of any election, upon the success or failure of any candidate or upon the number of votes be cast, either in the aggregate or any particular precinct, or upon the vote to any person is guilty of miscounting.

SEC. 2. Every person charged with violating the provisions of any law of this State relating to elections, who willfully elects or refuses to permit any official candidate, knowingly and fraudulently acts in confirmation or mitigation of any of the provisions of such laws shall be deemed guilty of felony, and punishable by fine not exceeding one thousand dollars, or by imprisonment in the STATE Prison not exceeding five years or by both such fine and imprisonment.

SEC. 3. Every person who, after being sworn, refuses to answer any pertinent question proffered by such Board touching his right or the right of any other person to vote, is guilty of miscounting, punishable by the fine of five hundred dollars, or imprisonment in the County Jail not exceeding three months or by both such fine and imprisonment.

SEC. 4. Every person not entitled to vote who fraudulently votes, and every person who seeks to vote than at any election, or knowingly hands two or more ballots together, or changes an ballot after the same has been deposited in the ballot box; and any person who adds any ballot to those legally polled at any election either by fraudulently introducing the same into the ballot box before the ballots therein have been counted, or adds any ballot with, or attempts to add to or mix with the ballots lawfully provided, other ballots while the same being counted canvass, abstracts any ballots lawfully polled at any other time with intent to change the result of each election, or carries away or destroys or attempts to carry away or destroy any poll list or ballots, ballot box, for the purpose of breaking up or invalidating such election or destroys, mutilates, or destroys any election returns, in any manner so interferes with the officers holding such election or conducting such canvass with voters lawfully exercising their right of voting at such election as to prevent such election or canvass from being fairly held and lawfully conducted shall be guilty of felony, punishable by fine not exceeding one thousand dollars, by imprisonment in the State Prison not exceeding five years, or by both such fine and imprisonment.

SEC. 5. Every person not entitled to vote who fraudulently attempts to vote, or who being entitled to vote, shall attempt, aids, assists, induces, advises or offers to hire or offer his services to any person in any election, moving that he be not qualified to vote, shall be guilty of a misdemeanor, punishable by the fine of two hundred dollars, as is imprisonment in the County Jail not exceeding six days or by both such fine and imprisonment.

SEC. 6. Every person who, in any election, shall in any manner mark the ballot in such a manner as to distinguish said ballot, or any mark in such ballot, with any stuff including ballot in any manner which has been intended to be cleaned or erased, previous to the casting of the same into a ballot box, or makes any mark or device on any valid ballot, with view to ascertaining the vote for any person for whom the elector has voted, or who, without the consent of the elector, lists in name any person which such elector, Judge or Clerk has fraudulently or falsely discovered to have voted for, shall be punishable by a fine of not less than five hundred dollars. the winter provided no large wounds are
made. An orchard properly and timely at-
tended to will rarely require the removal of
&c limbs. We often see recommendations

spring; and if trouble is likely to occur from

This is an application or the part OF Hon.
E. Staes, Justice of the Second Munlc1pal
Police Court of the city Of New Orleans,
for the exercise of the authority OF thus
court 20 enforce the performance OF duty
imposed by law on the sheriff OF the crlm-
inal courts. The facts upon which the ap-
plication is based briefly stated, are: That
one Esteban Riguelmy was arre sted under
the provisions of law enacted Dy the
General Assembly of the State at the ses-
sion held in the year 1874 known as act No.
9, which act imposes certain restrictions
upon the sale of lottery tickets within the
limits Of the city OF New Orleans and pro-
vides that a penalty shall be inflicted upon
any one violating the provisions Of said
act. and the jurisdiction to determine cases
arising under said act and to enforce
the penalty is given TO the police magls-
trates of the city of New Orleans. Alter
an examination IN the customary manner,
before the Ielato-. Rigueimy, was ad.
Judged guilty of violation OF the law, and
sentenced to pay fine OF twenty-five dol
lara, and, in default OF payment, to be com
| m;tted to the Parish Prison tor the space OF
i've davs The fine not being paid, the
said Riguelmy was delivered over to the
sheriff of the criminal courts as keeper OF
the Parish Prison, and he was commanded
to hold in custody this said Riguelmy, in
accordance with the sentence. WITHIN a
few moments after the disposition OF the
case by the~relator, Riguelmy, through his
| counsel, applied to the judge OF the Sixth
District Court tor writ of habeas corpus.
commanding the sheriff of the criminal
courts to produce the said Riguelmy IN
| that court: the sheriff complied with the
| order, and, upon the party appearing be-
| fore him, the Judge of the Sixth DistrIct
| Court, without hearing any argument on
| the question, discharged Rlguelmy upon the
| ground that he had, on several occasions,
prior to the present. declared that the law
| under which the relator acted was uncon-
| stitutiOnaI The relatOr, believing that the
| Judge of the Sixth District Court had acted
without any jurisdiction, and that great
wrong was being perpetrated 5y setting at
naught the authority of tne police magls'
trates, who, though possessing limited ]u-
risdiction. to the extent OF that lurlsdic-
| ton. are the representatives of the State,
| and also believing that the sheriff OF the
| criminal courts had obeyed an illegal order
| in releasing the party he was commanded
| tn hold in custody, has asked the interven-
| ton of this court to compel performance
| of duty BY an officer who is under the con-
| troll of this court, more so than under that
| of the First District Court, because this
l court LAS 5DCCldA pO"OAo SOiAAo@Aou NCNA ~
| that the latter court can not exercise.


This court has the authority to issue the
writ of mandamus. The question is, can
that writ be invoked under the state Of
facts supporting this application. Inc
Legislature, in creating this court, had IN
view the necessity Of a criminal court
having all the necessary jurisdiction,
aud hence, in the first section OF the
act establishing the court, 1t ls provided


This court shall have all the powers and
duties of court of highest criminal juris-
diction at common law" This
court shal. have power to Issue wrlts OF
habeas corpus for all purposes OF said writ;
also writs of mandamus, and all other wrlts
and processes necessary or Incidental to the
exercise and enforcement OF its lurlsdlc-
ton" Hence it is apparent that the Jurls-
diction of this court is not restricted to the
narrow limits within which the First Dis
trict has been and is obliged to act. Let it
not be understood that any extraordinary
authority is claimed for the Superior Crimi-
nal Court, but that it has all nessary juris-
diction for court of its character.


We need not go to the common law for
definition OF what constitutes the writ OF
mandamus. The Code Of Practice speaks
of it in article S2S as an "Order directing
the performance of some specific act Ar
ticle $50 saws: ''The object of this order is
| to prevent a denial of justice, or the oOnse-
| uuence of detective police, and it should
therefore be issued in all cases where the
law has assigned no relief by the ordinary
means. and where justice and reason require
that some mode should exist OF redressing
a wrong, or an abuse of any nature, what
ever" Art. S34. "It may be directed to
public officers to compel them to fulfil any
| of the duties attaceed to their office, OF
which may be legally required Of them"


Article ninety three OF the constitution OF
this State contains the following provision:
"In the parish Of Orleans there shall be
elected by the qualiyed voters OF the parish
! at large, one sheriff for the Criminal Court,
who shall be the executive officer of said
court. and shall have charge OF the Parish
Prison" Section three of the act creating
this court provides, "That the the sheriff
of the Criminal Court for the parish of Or
leans shall also be the sheriff and executive
officer of the Superior Criminal Court "
Under sections 1892 and 3393 OF the ne
| yised Statutes, the several judges OF this
State are given general supervisory control
over the executive officers OF their courts,
and these officers may he either fined or
suspended by the court having jurisdiction
| over them, tor disObeying not only the
orders of the court of which they. are the
executive officer, but OF courts that have
TIE authority to exact from them
any duty. 1t becomes apparent,





been quoted that this court has the
power to exercise sufficient control over
the sheriff of the criminal courts to compel
a proper performance of any duties I'M
posed upon him by law, and that the writ
of mandamus can be properly invoked for
that purpose. 1t is erroneous to suppose
that there must be some case pending before
the court in which the writ is to be avalled
of. The proceedings in reference to man
i 5o,rs .ra ORIGINAL. they constitute the
case; were it otherwise no writ OF man
damus could ever issue.

COLORALIA WASH—The following is a most excellent, cheap, and durable wash for wooden fences and buildings. It owes its durability chiefly to the lime, which hardens and fixes the wash: Take 1 barrel and slake one bushel of freshly burned lime in it, by covering the lime with boiling water. After it is slaked, add cold water enough to thin it to that consistency of good whitewash. STATEMENT TO THE PUBLIC.

Having felt it my duty to issue my proclamation offering a large reward for the apprehension and conviction OF the murderers in the Coushatta outrage, and to the end that the law-abiding citizens of the State may fully comprehend the magnitude of the crime committed, and be induced to render more active assistance to the officers of the law, I deem it proper to make the following statement. These facts are gathered from reliable information received at the executive department:

On or about the 28th day of August, 1874 body of persons belonging to a semi-military organization known as the White League of Louisiana assembled IN the town of Coushatta, parish OF Red River, this State, for the purpose of compelling by force of arms the State officials OF that parish to resign their positions. These officers were men OF good character, most of them largely interested in planting and mercantile pursuits. They held their positions with the full consent of an admittedly large majority OF the legal voters of the parish, this being a heavily Republican parish, as admitted by the fusion returning boards. The only known objection to them was that they were of Republican principles. Frank Edgerton, the duly qualified sheriff OF the parish, in strict compliance with the laws of this State and of the United States, summoned posse comitatus of citizens, white and colored, to assist him in protecting the parish officers in the exercise of their undoubted rights and duties from the White League. To THE Editor of the New York Times.


In your recent report on Dr. Stephen Smith's Christian Association Aquarium needing, and these assertions:


"Alcohol condemns with united voices all women, because it is a poison in the stomach of women as a food."


This is news, indeed, to some of us. Of course, no one wants women to use alcoholic beverage. No human being does use alcohol as a beverage except perhaps the Russian peasants, whose diet consists very much like ordinary "sip of wine." But the doctor, using the usual inaccurate fashion of the Aquarium, uses "alcohol or any LIQUID containing alcohol, no matter how small the percentage." When his statements are thus reduced to rational English, they are, repeat it, news to some of us. There are plenty of men, both professional and lay, who do not condemn or forbid the use of liquids containing alcohol as beverages by women, and every man who believes that alcohol in a man's stomach may act as food by making a smaller quantity of food more valuable (just as wood dust may partially replace log in the manufacture of paper), believes that it performs the same office in a woman's stomach.


Does DR. Smith mean by no man no American man, or does he make the statement universally, when he tells us scrupulously that no Englishman admits the propriety of a woman's drinking any beverage which contains alcohol? Surely he must know that the majority of English women, whose means permit it, are wine or beer drinkers, and that they are fine physical specimens. How many of our women can walk as they do? How many can sit horse over three feet of lumber? Many doctors will tell you that it is not safe for American women to ride at all; and it certainly seems impossible for many of them to walk any distance without fatigue and suffering. Now, I admit that the climate counts for something, but may not the diet count for something, too! And why does the English woman, as a general rule, eat more, and more nourishing food than the American woman? Not only because she takes more exercise in the open air, but because she uses those alcoholic beverages so abhorred by the Aquarium. I have often observed in our own country that when a lady, young or old, drank some claret or malt liquor with her dinner, she made a better and heartier meal.

President Grant's Views on the Money Question.

WASHINGTON, June 3.
Senator Jones has obtained permission from President Grant to publish the following memorandum prepared by the latter, expressing his views upon the money question. The President says:

I believe it a high and plain duty to return to a specie basis at the earliest practicable day, not only in compliance with legislative and party pledges, but as a step indispensable to lasting national prosperity. I believe, further, That the time has come when this can be done, or at least be begun, with less embarrassment to every branch of industry than at any future time, after resort has been made to unstable and temporary expedients to stimulate unreal prosperity and speculation on basis of other than coin, the recognized medium of exchange throughout the commercial world. In particular, the mode selected to bring about restoration of the specie standard is not of so much consequence as that some adequate plan be devised, time fixed when the currency shall be exchangeable for coin at par, and a plan adopted and rigidly adhered to. It is not probable that any legislation suggested by me would prove acceptable to both branches of Congress, and, indeed full discussion might shake my own faith in the details of any plan I might propose.

"And noting," I state, "the salient features of action which seem to me advisable, the financial platform on which I would stand, and any departure from which would be in a spirit of concession and harmony in difference to conflicting opinions:

1. I would like to see the legal-tender clause, so-called, repealed; the repeal to take effect at some future time, say July 1, 1875. This would cause all contracts made after that date for wages, sales, etc., to be estimated in coin; it would correct our notions of values: the specie dollar would be the only dollar known as the measure of equivalents. When debts afterward contracted were paid in currency, instead of calling a paper dollar a dollar and quoting gold at so much premium, we should think and speak of paper as at so much discount. This alone would aid greatly in bringing the two currencies nearer together at par.

2. I would like to see a provision that at a fixed day, say July 1, 1876, the currency issued by the United States should be redeemed in coin on presentation to any assistant-treasurer, and that all currency so redeemed should be cancelled and never reissued. To effect this it would be necessary to authorize the issue of bonds payable in gold, bearing such interest as would command par in gold, to be put out by the Treasury only in such sums as should from time to time be needed for the purpose of redemption.

Such legislation would insure return to sound financial principles in two years, and would, in my judgment, work less hardship to the debtor interest than is likely to come from putting off the day of final reckoning. It must be borne in mind, too, that the creditor interest had its day of disadvantage also when our present financial system was brought in by the supreme needs of the nation at the time.

I would further provide that, from and after the date fixed for redemption, no bills, whether of national banks or of the United States, returned to the Treasury to be exchanged for new bills, should be replaced by bills of less denomination than ten dollars, and that in one year after resumption all bills of less than five dollars should be withdrawn from circulation, and in two years all bills of less than ten dollars should be withdrawn. The advantage of this would be the strength given to the country against time of depression resulting from war, failure of the crops, or any other cause, by keeping always in the hands of the people large supply of precious metals. Transactions conducted in coin, many millions of it would be kept in constant use, and, of course, prevented from leaving the country. Undoubtedly poorer currency will always drive the better out of circulation. With paper legal tender and at a discount gold and silver become articles of merchandise as much as wheat or cotton.

The surplus will find the best market it can. With small bills in circulation there is no use for coin except to keep it in the vaults of banks to redeem circulation. During periods of great speculation and apparent prosperity there is little demand for coin, and then it will flow out to a market where it can be made to earn something, which it cannot do while lying idle. Gold, like anything else, when not needed becomes a surplus, and like every other surplus it seeks a market where it can find one. By giving it active employment, however, its presence can, it seems to me, be secured, and panics and depressions which have occurred periodically in times of nominal specie payments, if they cannot be wholly prevented, can at least be greatly mitigated. Indeed, I question whether it would have been found necessary to depart from the standard of specie in the trying days which gave birth to the first Legal-Tender act had the country taken the ground of no small bills as early as 1850.

Again, I would provide an excess of revenue over current expenditures. I would do this by rigid economy and by taxation where taxation can best be borne. Increased revenue would work a constant reduction of the debt and interest and would provide coin to meet the demands on the Treasury for redemption of its notes, thereby diminishing the amount of bonds needed for that purpose.

All taxes after redemption begins should be paid in coin or United States notes. This would force redemption on the national banks.

With measures like these, or measures which would work out such results, I see no danger in authorizing free banking without limit."

A MERRY AFTERNOON AT THE NEWSBOY'S LODGING-HOUSE


RIVINGTON-ST. LODGING-HOUSES


Ample preparations were made at the Newsboy's Lodging house in New York for the boys' good Thanksgiving dinner. Contributions received for this object were much more in amount than they were last year, thus lessening the burden of expense upon the Society. The dinner was an excellent one. About 500 pounds of turkeys and chickens were provided together with pies, cakes, coffee, and tea in abundance. Mr. O'Connor, the superintendent, and his assistants took great pains to give the dining-room and the long tables a neat and tasteful appearance. About 4 o'clock from all the lower wards of the city the ragged urchins began to troop in to feast. Before entering the dining-hall they were obliged to repair to the bathrooms, from which they emerged transformed in personal appearance—their dusty clothes brushed, their unkempt hair combed, and their hands and faces clean. There were no speeches to detain the hungry little fellows from their meal, but fast—they sat down and they began the long rows of stuffing turkeys and chickens, the fat pies, the gay frosted cakes and hot coffee set before them. Their hilarity was unrestrained and they laughed and joked and ate to their hearts' content. Some of them had evidently dressed for the occasion. Their ragged clothes were neatly pinned into shapeliness, new paper cleaned under their ears, and bright-colored ribbons served for neckties. Several visitors came to watch, but the boys did not want to be interrupted and snubbed visitors who attempted to draw them into necessary conversation. "Those little fellows said to the SUPERINTENDENT, 'have a good deal of pride and self-respect. They think they pay for what they get and they don't like to be looked upon as the recipients of charity.' They quickly resent any attempt to make a show of them. They think they have a right to eat their Thanksgiving dinner undisturbed and think so too." The total number of boys fed yesterday was about 100 more than last year. After dinner many of the little fellows went into the gymnasium, a large room well fitted and provided with all the usual apparatus. Here they enjoyed themselves for an hour or two and then went to bed. The dormitories will accommodate about 800 sleepers and the rooms were well filled last night. The managers of the institution, especially the superintendent, who has long been connected with this particular charity, are acquainted with nearly every streetboy in the city, and know the needs of almost every one that applies to them. Those who enjoyed the dinner and the amusements furnished at the Newsboys' Lodging-house last night were all poor boys, who earn a livelihood principally by selling newspapers and walking posts. Most of them regular dodgers, but strange boys who came were not turned away hungry but made welcome not only by the managers but by those who shared their Thanksgiving dinner. The newsboys have another good dinner to look forward to which will be prepared for them on Christmas by private bounty.


At the Rivington Street Lodging-house for Boys last evening a dinner was given by Henry Hawley and W. L. and A. L. Smith to the lodgers who are mostly boot blacks and newsboys. The school and dining-rooms were neatly and tastefully decorated with flowers and evergreens and presented an attractive appearance. On the desk in the school-room a handsome aquarium was placed. It was an interesting sight to watch the eager faces of the boys; they sat as though their anxiety to taste the good things prepared for them could not be concealed. At 12 o'clock the exercises opened. The boys sang several hymns with voices and feeling, and addresses were made by the Rev. Mr. Goss and the Rev. Mr. Linphler. Close attention was paid to the speakers, who were told they would be brief. Then, under the direction of George Calder, the Superintendent, the boys formed in line and quietly marched to the dining-room below. There was about 40 pounds of roast turkey and plum pudding and cakes, pies and oranges in abundance. Their meal was very credible, and attracted the attention, and called forth the approbation of all. The visitors were more than was too often seen on similar occasions. Just at the close of the meal, several came in and were received with thanks.

Music was also provided, and several pieces were played by Mr. White, who played several pieces of music on the piano. George T. Miller had formerly taken the boys of the Lodging-house on excursions, then made a short address. He was enthusiastically received and spoke of his long acquaintance with almost everybody here; he said that success was only gained by patience and perseverance. His remarks were therefore well received and the pleasure of the boys was great. He said he would long remember the kindness of these newsboys.

A substantial dish of fruit was given yesterday; the pies and cakes were taken home, at which the Rev. Father John Drunell had invited a number of the older boys had left the institution and they, with the others, assembled in the hall, where he made a brief address in welcoming words. They heartily and joyously shared the festivities.

the announcement of the death of Senator
Charles Sumner, of Massachusetts, after an
illness of less than a day. Senator Sumner
occupied his seat in the Senate on Tuesday,

the nerves of the heart, but when he returned
home he was sufficiently well to entertain two
friends at dinner, at the close of which he
made allusion to the condition of his heart;
and between 9 and 10 o'clock he was taken so
sick as to require the attendance of a physician.
An hour or more thereafter he had a second
attack of his old disease, angina pectoris, and
from that time rapidly sank until death occur
red, at 2.45 Wednesday afternoon. Numerous
friends surrounded the bedside of the re-
nowned Senator, who retained his conscious
ness to the last, recognizing the voices of
those who spoke to him, although he declared
his inability to see them. Charles Sumner
was born in Boston, January 6, 1811, gradu
ated at Harvard College in 1832 and studied
law in the same institution after taking his
degree. In early life he contributed to and
afterward became editor of the American
Jurist. In 1834 he was admitted to the bar
and began to practice law in Boston. He ed
ited, in 1836, Dunlop's Treatise on the
Practice of the Admiralty Courts in Cases of
Civil Jurisdiction at Sea. In 1837, he
visited Europe and at the request of Gen.
Cass, French Ambassador, wrote a defense of
the rights of the United States in reference
to the questions then pending between the
two governments. Mr. Sumner signalized
himself by his opposition to the annexation of
Texas, and by his support of Mr. Van Buren,
as candidate for the Presidency in 1836, and
was elected to the U. S. Senate, as successor
of Daniel Webster, in 1853. He was a famous
champion of slave abolition, and the leader of
the radical party with that object in view.

radicalism on the question of slavery, ac-
quired a national reputation, than by the
brutal assault made upon him in 1856, by
Brooks of South Carolina in the Senate
Chamber, where he was beaten down and lay
weltering in his blood. He recommended the

fair, whilst maintaining that English prece-
dents were favorable to the right of the United
States government to retain them. In 1859

den's rider, Vesuvius, until it looked as if she
might win the race. But the picture changed in
the green hedge of a hurdle. Tabitha lifted her
forelegs and made her leap, and then came down
in a broken error mass. There was a
vapor and there picture of lad in a
lilac jacket running off to the fence, while the
noble animal lay there, her left hind leg smashed,

and low down, and it hung by mere shreds of
flesh, while the blood slowly formed a pool around

asked stout young Irish lad named Jim Dowd

and blood came flowing in red stream from the
nostrils. The crowd widened out a little, some
one crying out, "Let him have room!" and in few
short moments the gallant Tabitha was as dead
as good hail, another monument to the folly and
crime of hurdle racing. But what matters the

counted. If both clauses be erased, or neither
clause be erased, the vote upon the subject shall
not be counted.


The residence Of Hugh Smith was burglarized on Wednesday night. A watch
and pocketbook were taken. The pocketbook was empty, and the watch was valued at $50. The thief entered by means
of an open window.


A day or two ago a Mr. Anderson, who
lives on the pike opposite Berry's rope
store, two miles west of Bridgeport, with
his family left home upon a visit, leaving
no one in care of the house. A notorious
woman named Criswell entered the
house and appropriated several articles
of jewelry in the absence of the proprietor. On Wednesday evening she was
arrested near Martins Ferry by Deputy
Marshal Reese Burdet, and after a preliminary hearing before Mayor McConnaughty, was taken to St. Clairsville and
lodged in Jail to await trial.


Henry Harrison, an old Bridgeport boy,
who has been in Missouri for a number of
years, is at home on visit.


The Women's Temperance Band held a
meeting in the Presbyterian Church yesterday afternoon. Ladies were present
from St. Clairsville, Bellaire and Martins
Ferry. The meeting was very interesting and enthusiastic, but the proceedings
have not been made public. Last evening Dr. J. N. J. Kelley, of the Fourth Street
N. E. Church, addressed an open all
meeting from the steps of the Bank.


The dog ordinance recently passed by
the Bridgeport Council went into effect
on Wednesday, and the Marshal notified
all owners of canines to pay the tax.
During the day he gathered in seventeen dogs upon which no tax was paid
and locked them up in the jail. What
disposition was made of the innocent ones
We have not learned.


A number of Bridgeporters last night
attended a social dance at Norris Grove
just beyond St. Clairsville. Bryan's
Quadrille Band furnished the music for
the occasion.


Another highly colored sensation supplied Bridgeporters with gossip on
Wednesday evening. John Sawyer, who
is colored, is also a gay Lothario. He
was promenading and whispering his love
into the sunburnt ear of his divinity, when
he was suddenly startled by a shrill voice
which he knew, alas too well, crying
out, "Are you satisfied, now that you
got him?" It was Becky Blanchard with
whom he spoke. Becky is about the color of a
traditional ace of diamonds, and resides
in Martins Ferry. She was sweet
on John, who had told her his
love upon several occasions. However, when she called to him, John told
her to "cheese it." She replied that although fair he was false—and good deal
more. John became angry, and pushed
her. Then Becky's maidenly modesty
did not forsake her. She cast rocks at
John fast and freely. The gay deceiver
escaped with his gazelle uninjured.
A man named John Williams, who had just
arrived on the 6 o'clock train to go to
work at the Kanawha Mill, was hit in the
head by a stone thrown by the irate
Becky. He received an ugly cash mark
immediately over his right eye. It was a rather
warm welcome for Williams—but he
should never have went to Bridgeport.
No arrests were made, and all is again
serene.
